summary:
ANANT is a zero-install, browser-based 3D exoplanet exploration and orbital reconnaissance simulator developed by Team Ananth Tandav. Built using WebGL and procedural planetary generation, ANANT allows users to pilot the DSN reconnaissance probe ANANT-01 across real-scale star systems modeled after confirmed NASA mission targets, including the TRAPPIST-1 system, Kepler-452b, and Proxima Centauri b.

Traditional exoplanet catalogs present discovery metrics as static tables, making it difficult for students and the public to grasp orbital scale, atmospheric scattering, and planetary scale. ANANT transforms NASA Exoplanet Archive parameters and JPL Horizons ephemeris concepts into an interactive, real-time flight experience complete with Deep Space Network telemetry overlays and surface flyby missions. By running directly in any modern web browser without heavy downloads, ANANT democratizes access to realistic exoplanetary science and space mission simulation.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

ANANT is an interactive 3D spaceflight and planetary survey simulation accessible directly through a web browser. Players command the ANANT-01 reconnaissance probe across multi-body star systems, executing orbital insertions, atmospheric grazing maneuvers, and low-altitude surface inspections. The simulation renders real-time planetary terrain, atmospheric Rayleigh/Mie scattering horizons, and orbital trajectories paired with a NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) telemetry HUD.

Tools, Languages & Architecture

  • Core Engine & Rendering: TypeScript, WebGL / Babylon.js procedural planetary and shader pipeline.
  • UI & Telemetry Layer: HTML5, CSS3, custom high-contrast monospace telemetry overlay modeled after JPL flight instrumentation.
  • Deployment: Static web bundle hosted for instant, zero-install browser access across desktop devices.

Intended Impact & Creativity Rather than treating exoplanet discovery as passive data visualization, ANANT bridges scientific catalog parameters with tactile spatial exploration. Users experience the true scale difference between red dwarf habitable-zone worlds (such as TRAPPIST-1e and TRAPPIST-1f) and super-Earths (Kepler-452b). Because it requires zero installation and runs smoothly on standard laptops, educators, students, and space enthusiasts can immediately explore distant worlds and understand orbital mechanics firsthand.

Design Considerations Our team prioritized zero-friction accessibility, visual clarity, and scientific grounding—stripping away cluttered controls in favor of clean telemetry readouts and curated mission scenarios (Project Lazarus: Habitable Zone Recon, TRAPPIST-1e Atmospheric Survey, and Europa Cryo-Surface Scan).
